title: Logic Modeling of Signaling Networks
markdown: ## What this covers Real signaling networks are too large, and too sparsely measured, to write down as a system of chemical rate equations. This chapter works through an alternative: build a wiring diagram from the literature, turn each arrow into a logic gate (activating, inhibiting, AND, OR), and fit the gates' few free parameters to combinatorial perturbation data. The running example is a network of cytokine and growth-factor signaling in liver cells, trained with *constrained fuzzy logic* and then used to compare a normal cell line against several liver-cancer lines. It assumes familiarity with a signal-transduction cascade (receptor, kinase cascade, transcription factor) and with Boolean AND/OR/NOT; no differential equations are assumed, since avoiding them is exactly the point. This lecture was given entirely over slides — no transcript was supplied for it — so everything below traces to a specific figure rather than to a spoken argument. ## Why not model the kinetics directly A signaling network, drawn out in full, looks less like a pathway than a printed circuit board: one of the deck's slides makes this literal, showing genes and proteins soldered onto a circuit board in place of resistors and transistors. Reconstructions of the interactions around a single receptor bear this out — a map of everything reported to interact with EGFR is a "hairball" of several hundred nodes and thousands of edges, and that is one receptor's neighborhood, assembled from databases the deck names explicitly (the NCI-Nature Pathway Interaction Database, I2D, NetPath, and KEGG), which between them catalog many more such neighborhoods. Writing a validated rate equation, with a measured rate constant, for every edge in a network of that size is not a research programme that finishes. It is also not obviously the right unit of description, even where the kinetics could be measured. A genomic survey of pancreatic tumors shown in the deck makes the point sharply: each tumor carries tens to well over a hundred somatic mutations, amplifications and deletions, and two tumors can share almost none of the same mutated genes — yet the mutations recur, tumor after tumor, in the same dozen or so pathway categories (K-Ras signaling, Wnt/Notch signaling, control of the G1/S transition, apoptosis, DNA-damage control, invasion, and so on). The disease-relevant object is which pathways are perturbed, not which specific gene did the perturbing in a given patient. That argues for building a model at the level of pathway topology and its logic, rather than at the level of one protein's binding kinetics — coarser, but pitched at the level where the biology actually seems to repeat. The deck states this trade-off directly, under the heading "model family precision generally presages accuracy," crediting the accompanying figure to Morris et al. (2011). That figure did not survive this conversion, so it is named here rather than described, but the principle it illustrates is worth carrying through the rest of the chapter: a model built to a coarse standard should be trusted only for correspondingly coarse conclusions, and that is a feature of logic models to keep in view, not a limitation to apologize for. ## Building the network: cues, signals, and responses The case study developed through the rest of the lecture is a network of cytokine and growth-factor signaling in liver cells. It has three layers. Cues are extracellular ligands — in this network, IL-6, IFN-γ, TGF-α, IGF-1, TNF-α, IL-1α and LPS — each with its own receptor. Signals are the several dozen intracellular signaling proteins downstream of those receptors: kinases such as AKT, ERK, JNK, p38 and IKK, and downstream targets such as STAT3, c-Jun, CREB and p53, each measurable — typically as a phosphorylation level — at a series of time points. Responses are what the cell does as a result: here, the secretion of dozens of inflammatory, anti-inflammatory, chemokine, and growth cytokines. The deck's own one-line summary of the whole chapter is exactly this structure: extracellular ligand cues, then signals, then a response (phenotype). Crucially, the wiring between these layers is not measured directly for this purpose. It is assembled from the literature — hundreds of individually published claims of the form "A activates B" or "A inhibits B," compiled into one large diagram the same way a textbook pathway figure is compiled, except kept as a formal graph rather than a picture. This literature-derived graph is usually called a prior knowledge network: a hypothesis about topology, fixed before any of the group's own data is brought to bear on it. ## From wiring diagram to logic gates A prior knowledge network only says which nodes are connected and whether the edge is activating or inhibiting. To turn it into something that predicts a signal from a set of cues, every node needs a rule for combining its regulators. The simplest such rule is Boolean: assign every node a value of 0 (inactive) or 1 (active), and combine multiple regulators of the same node with AND, OR, and NOT. A concrete example from the deck's cross-cell-line comparison: IKK is drawn as activated by MAP3K1 AND NIK together — neither input on its own is enough, both are needed for the output to switch on. NOT is how the deck represents inhibition throughout — GSK3, for instance, is switched off by AKT rather than switched on by it. Boolean logic is the right level of abstraction for the topology, but it throws away everything the phosphoprotein assays actually measure. A phosphorylation signal is not simply on or off; it rises and falls continuously, by different amounts under different stimuli, and the deck's own classification of the training responses has four categories — absent, transient, sustained, late — not two. Fitting a Boolean network to graded, noisy, time-resolved data needs a continuous stand-in for each Boolean gate. ## Making the gates continuous: constrained fuzzy logic The fix used throughout this case study — constrained fuzzy logic — replaces each Boolean edge with a Hill function of the same shape used for cooperative binding curves, and each Boolean AND/OR with the minimum or maximum of the corresponding Hill functions. For a single regulator $a$ acting on a node $c$, both normalized to lie in $[0,1]$, an activating edge is $$c = (k^n + 1)\frac{a^n}{k^n + a^n}$$ and an inhibiting edge is $$c = 1 - (k^n + 1)\frac{a^n}{k^n + a^n},$$ where $n$ is a Hill coefficient controlling how switch-like the edge is, and $k$ sets the half-maximal point of that edge (an EC50). When a node has two regulators $a$ and $b$, each transformed by its own Hill function $f_1$ and $f_2$ with their own $n$ and $k$, the two Boolean gates become continuous by taking the minimum or the maximum of the two: $$c = \min\left(f_1(a),\ f_2(b)\right) \qquad \text{for AND,}$$ $$c = \max\left(f_1(a),\ f_2(b)\right) \qquad \text{for OR.}$$ This is exactly the "logic" in logic modeling: the topology and the gate type (AND/OR/NOT) at every node are fixed by the literature-derived network, and only the handful of Hill-function parameters per edge are left free to be estimated from data — one or two numbers per edge, rather than a full set of rate constants and initial conditions, while still producing continuous, graded predictions rather than a lookup table of 0s and 1s. ## Fitting the gates to data The parameters are fit against a combinatorial perturbation experiment: cells are treated with each ligand crossed with a panel of kinase inhibitors — in the deck's training data, inhibitors of MEK1/2, p38, PI3K, IKK, mTOR, GSK3α/β and JNK1/2, plus a no-inhibitor control — and roughly a dozen and a half phosphoprotein signals are measured over time in each condition. Fitting means choosing every edge's $n$ and $k$ so that propagating each cue forward through the network of gates reproduces the measured time course of every signal, across every one of those conditions simultaneously — a single set of edge parameters has to explain the whole grid at once, which is what makes the fit informative rather than a separate curve fit per condition. ## The fit is not unique A network this size, fit against a finite and noisy dataset, does not have one best-fitting answer. The deck shows this directly: relaxing the fit's error tolerance from 0% to a still-modest 47% increases the number of qualitatively different edge-parameter solutions that satisfy it from 9 to 97. Put differently, even a fairly narrow band of "acceptably good fits" already contains dozens of networks that disagree with each other about the strength, or even the presence, of some edges, while explaining the training data about equally well. This is a standard feature of fitting a richly parameterized model to a finite dataset — non-identifiability — and it means a single fitted network should never be reported as *the* answer; what a dataset like this supports is a family, or ensemble, of comparably good models. ## How much to trust a prediction Since no single model is privileged, a prediction from a fit like this needs its own measure of confidence, and the deck builds one from two independent axes: how much the models in the ensemble agree with each other on a given prediction (measured by the coefficient of variation, CV, across the ensemble) and how close that prediction lands to held-out test data (mean squared error, MSE). Crossing these gives four outcomes: models can agree and be right, agree and be wrong, disagree yet still land close to the truth, or disagree and be wrong. The deck's own test predictions scatter across this space rather than clustering in the reassuring corner — IκB's predicted response to TNF-α, for instance, sits at both high disagreement and high error, the worst combination, while p53's predicted response to TNF-α sits at just as high a disagreement but low error, meaning the ensemble members disagree with each other yet happen to bracket the right answer. The lesson generalizes beyond this one network: agreement among an ensemble of models is not, by itself, evidence that the ensemble is correct, and checking that requires data the fit did not see. ## Validating on combinations the model never saw The strongest test offered in the deck is prediction, not fit: the trained model — built from single-ligand, single-inhibitor training data — is asked to predict the phosphoprotein response to combinations of ligands (single cytokines, and pairs of them together) crossed with combinations of up to five inhibitors (targeting MEK, p38, PI3K, IKK and EGFR) that were not part of the training grid. The deck reports that the qualitative response pattern predicted for these held-out combinations matches the measured one closely across the panel — evidence that a model built only to reproduce single-perturbation data already captures enough of the network's combinatorial logic to generalize to combinations, which is the point of building a mechanistic model rather than simply interpolating a training table. ## The same network, fit to five cell lines The clearest payoff of this approach shows up when the same prior-knowledge network, with the same topology, is fit separately to five different cell lines: primary human hepatocytes, and four hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer) lines — HepG2, Hep3B, Huh7 and Focus. Two results follow. First, a model trained on one cell line's data explains that same cell line's held-out data best (a residual error typically in the range of roughly 0.09–0.20 in the deck's units) and explains another cell line's data distinctly worse — cross-fitting a model to the wrong cell line roughly doubles the error. That is a signature of real rewiring between cell types, not of noisy fitting: if the five cell lines all shared one logic network and differed only in measurement noise, one model should serve all five about equally well, and it clearly does not. The clearest single miss in the deck's own error breakdown by cue and signal is IL-6's effect on STAT3, whose residual sits near the top of the scale while almost every other cue/signal pair in the same matrix fits comfortably below it. Second, building a "distance" between cell lines out of these cross-fit errors shows the four cancer lines sitting closer to each other than any of them sits to the primary cells — the rewiring is not each cancer line drifting off in its own idiosyncratic direction, but several cancer lines drifting in a broadly shared direction, away from normal. This is corroborated independently: clustering the five cell lines by how similar their *fitted logic models* are reproduces the same split into an epithelial group (Focus) and a mesenchymal group (Huh7, Hep3B, HepG2) that an entirely separate measurement, gene expression, also produces, with primary cells as the outgroup in both. Two unrelated measurements agreeing on the same grouping is good evidence that the differences the logic model is picking up are biological, not an artifact of the fitting procedure. The deck also points to specific rewired edges rather than leaving the claim at "the networks differ." In one such example (the deck's own Figure 5), an explicit AND gate feeding IKK — driven jointly by MAP3K1 and NIK — together with several edges along the insulin-receptor branch (the insulin receptor, IRS-1, and PI3K) and the AKT-to-GSK3 inhibitory edge, show materially different behavior between the primary cells and the cancer lines, including cases where IκB's response to TNF-α depends on PI3K in some cell lines but not others. ## A caveat: how clean are the perturbations The whole approach leans on pharmacological kinase inhibitors to perturb one node and see what changes downstream — the model attributes any resulting change entirely to loss of the targeted kinase's activity. The deck includes a direct check on that assumption: two inhibitors nominally targeting IKK, TPCA-1 and BMS-345541, were tested against both IKK-2 and Jak2, in vitro and in cells. Their potencies against IKK-2 differ by roughly an order of magnitude between the two inhibitors, and BMS-345541 also has measurable activity against Jak2 at concentrations used in the cell-based assay. An inhibitor that is not as selective as advertised will look, to the fitting procedure, exactly like a new or altered edge in the network — so a claimed rewired interaction is only as trustworthy as the selectivity of the tool used to find it, a caveat the fitting procedure itself has no way to catch. ## A different route to the same kind of data The deck closes with a study that uses the same style of experiment — a panel of phosphoprotein readouts measured over time across many treatment conditions — for a different purpose, without building a network model at all. Pritchard, Cosgrove, Hemann, Griffith, Wands and Lauffenburger (*Molecular Cancer Therapeutics*, 2009) profiled hepatocellular carcinoma cell lines treated with 17-AAG, a multi-targeted geldanamycin analogue (an Hsp90 inhibitor), across a panel including phospho-IκBα, phospho-AKT, phospho-GSK3, phospho-ERK, phospho-STAT3, phospho-JNK and phospho-p38. Rather than fitting a mechanistic network to this data, they ran a principal component analysis on it to find which handful of pathways accounted for most of the drug's multi-pathway signature, then picked a combination of three more selective inhibitors (targeting IKK, PI3K and Jak) aimed at just those pathways. In Huh7 cells, that three-inhibitor combination alone produced apoptosis (measured by cleaved caspase-3/cleaved PARP) at a level similar to or exceeding 17-AAG itself, while none of the three inhibitors alone, added to 17-AAG, came close. It is the same kind of combinatorial phosphoprotein dataset as the logic-modeling case study, put to a different use: instead of a mechanistic network that can be interrogated and validated on new combinations, a purely statistical decomposition of the same kind of data points directly at an actionable drug combination. ## Sources Everything above is drawn from a single slide deck, `lectures/17-slides.md` in `computational-biology/mit-ocw/7091j` (MIT 7.91J / 20.490J / 20.390J / 7.36J / 6.802J / 6.874J / HST.506J, Spring 2014).
